extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, occupational health and safety professionals, and stakeholders preparing comments to OSHA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed regulatory requirements for employers to prevent heat-related illness, including rest breaks, observation, hazard alerts, warning signs, emergency response planning, and training under the OSHA proposed heat standard (NPRM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory minimum rest breaks when high heat trigger met
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (f)(2) requires employers to ensure that employees have at least one break that lasts a minimum of 15 minutes every two hours when the high heat trigger is met or exceeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaks are mandatory, must be taken in the break area required under paragraph (e)(3) or (4), and the employer must ensure breaks are taken as required. The required break periods are a minimum; employers may provide longer or more frequent breaks. If an employee takes a rest break under paragraph (e)(8) lasting at least 15 consecutive minutes, that counts toward the (f)(2) requirement (example given: a 15-minute e(8) break taken in hour 1 removes the need for another f(2) break for the next two hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks must be paid
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraphs (f)(2) and (e)(8) require that employees be paid during rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA emphasizes payment so employees are not financially penalized and discouraged from taking breaks. See Explanation of Proposed Requirements for paragraph (j) for methods employers can use to ensure both hourly and piece-rate employees are compensated for rest breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a rest break (exclusions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest breaks are not the same as slowing down or pacing; performing a sedentary work activity, even in a compliant break area, would not be considered a rest break under the proposed standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed paragraphs (f)(2)(ii) and (iii) clarify that rest break time does not include time to put on/remove PPE or time to walk to/from the break area; OSHA finds it important to exclude donning/doffing and walking so employees have the full 15 minutes to cool down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meal break counting toward rest break
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (f)(2)(i) indicates that a meal break that is not required to be paid under law may count as a rest break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a meal break must be paid is governed by other laws (e.g., Fair Labor Standards Act, 29 CFR 785.19). To count, the meal period must be a bona fide meal period (typically 30 minutes or more) and the employee must be completely relieved from duties (not required to perform any duties while eating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer flexibility and operational approaches to provide rest breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA recognizes some employers may find providing a rest break every two hours challenging and suggests operational approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include staggering employee break times within the required two-hour period, providing portable shade structures where safe (consider elevation, wind), and scheduling work tasks during cooler parts of the day to reduce the need for breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation for signs and symptoms of heat-related illness (general requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (f)(3) requires employers to implement at least one of two methods of observing employees for signs and symptoms of heat-related illness, with a third option for employees who work alone at a work site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finds observation critical to identify early signs so appropriate action can be taken. The requirement is tied to the high heat trigger and interacts with training (paragraph (h)) and communications (paragraph (e)(9)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Buddy system option for observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under proposed paragraph (f)(3)(i), employers may implement a mandatory buddy system in which co-workers observe each other for signs and symptoms of heat-related illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buddies must be in the same work area so observation is possible. Co-workers may use visual cues, signs, and verbal communication to communicate signs and symptoms to one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor or heat safety coordinator observation option (limit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under proposed paragraph (f)(3)(ii), employers may have observation carried out by a supervisor or heat safety coordinator, but no more than 20 employees can be observed per supervisor/heat safety coordinator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors/coordintors must be positioned to observe employees (close enough to see and communicate) and be able to check in regularly (e.g., every two hours). They may have other tasks but must remain able to perform the observation role. OSHA preliminarily finds limiting the number to 20 necessary to ensure adequate observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation requirement for employees who work alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Under proposed paragraph (f)(3)(iii), for employees working alone at a work site, the employer must maintain a means of effective two-way communication with those employees and make contact with them at least every two hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must not only reach out but receive communication back from the lone employee; lack of response may indicate a problem. OSHA requests comment on logistical concerns and examples of successful two-way communication systems and technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: signs and symptoms of heat-related illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (b) defines 'Signs and symptoms of heat related illness' as the physiological manifestations of a heat-related illness and includes headache, nausea, weakness, dizziness, elevated body temperature, muscle cramps, and muscle pain or spasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA indicates employees should be asked about symptoms (some are not outwardly visible) and trained to report signs/symptoms they experience or observe in others (see proposed paragraph (h)(1)(x) training). Certain changes in behavior (working more slowly, dropping things) may indicate heat-related illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: signs and symptoms of a heat emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (b) defines 'signs and symptoms of a heat emergency' as physiological manifestations that require emergency response and includes loss of consciousness (fainting, collapse) with excessive body temperature, and may include vertigo, nausea, headache, cerebral dysfunction, bizarre behavior, staggering, vomiting, acting irrationally or disoriented, and convulsions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is used to identify when immediate emergency procedures are required under proposed paragraph (g)(3). OSHA requests comment on adding/removing items from the definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard alert requirement (timing and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (f)(4) would require employers to issue a hazard alert to employees prior to a work shift or when employees are exposed to heat at or above the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hazard alert must notify employees of: the importance of drinking plenty of water; employees' right to, at their election, take rest breaks if needed and the rest breaks required by paragraph (f)(2); how to seek help and procedures to take in a heat emergency; and for mobile worksites, the location of break areas and drinking water. If exposure will meet/exceed the high heat trigger at shift start, alert must be prior to shift; otherwise must be issued when trigger is met and ideally before exposure. Employers can presume electronic/regular communications are received unless they have reason to believe they were not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard alert delivery methods and comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may issue hazard alerts by posting signs, electronically (email/text), or verbally (in-person meeting, radio, voicemail), but the method must ensure all employees are notified and understand the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs may not be sufficient for mobile employees or lone workers and may not suffice if job starts below trigger and alert issued later. Hazard alert must be issued in languages and at a literacy level understood by employees. Employers may use systems in place for effective two-way communication (paragraph (e)(9)). OSHA requests comments on frequency and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning signs for excessively high heat areas (>120°F regularly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (f)(5) would require employers to place warning signs at indoor work areas with ambient temperatures that regularly exceed 120°F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs must be legible, visible, and understandable to employees entering the work area, located so employees can see them before entry, have adequate lighting, and not be blocked. Signs need not have specified contents but could include signal words (e.g., 'Danger'), hazard description ('High Heat Area'), possible health effects, access limitations ('Authorized Personnel Only'), and required precautions. Signs must be in a language(s) employees understand or employers must train employees to understand the signs. 'Regularly' means a pattern/frequency rather than isolated incidents (e.g., daily during certain seasons). Employers identifying heat hazards under paragraph (d) and (d)(3) monitoring plans will inform sign placement. Employers must train employees on procedures for these areas (see (h)(1)(xvi)). OSHA requests comment on wording/content and threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat emergency response plan required as part of HIIPP
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(1) requires employers to develop and implement a heat emergency response plan as part of their Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must seek input and involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives in plan development (paragraph (c)(6)). Only one plan is required per employer but it must be tailored to different work sites/types of work; elements may be combined into one plan with site-specific specifications. Employers may include additional elements beyond those required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements of the emergency response plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(1) specifies required elements employers must include in the emergency response plan: a list of emergency phone numbers; description of how employees can contact supervisor and EMS; designation of individual(s) to ensure procedures are invoked; description of how to transport employees to reach EMS; clear and precise directions to the work site (address/GPS); and procedures for responding to employees experiencing signs/symptoms, including suspected heat stroke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: include appropriate phone numbers (911, on-site clinicians), describe alternative communications (radios, walkie-talkies, personal locator beacons), designate persons for each work site or area if employer has multiple sites, plan for remote or frequently changing locations (GPS, directions), and use OSHA/NIOSH resources in developing procedures. The plan must contain all required information though some elements will vary by site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer actions when employee experiencing signs/symptoms of heat-related illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(2) requires employers to (i) relieve from duty employees experiencing signs/symptoms, (ii) monitor those employees, (iii) ensure they are not left alone, (iv) offer on-site first aid or medical services before ending monitoring, and (v) provide means to reduce body temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief from duty (including time to address the illness) must be with pay and continue at least until symptoms have subsided. Monitoring and not leaving employees alone ensures rapid response if condition worsens. First-aid offering is intended to be consistent with existing first-aid standards; employers are not required to have fully trained first-aid staff beyond existing obligations. Means to reduce body temperature include instructing removal of PPE/heavy outer clothing and moving to cooled/shaded areas (break areas under e(3)/(4)), or using on-site cooling PPE (cooling bandanas, vests, hybrid personal cooling systems, fans).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer actions during a heat emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(3) requires employers to take immediate actions to reduce the employee's body temperature before EMS arrives, contact EMS immediately, and perform the activities described in paragraphs (g)(2)(i)–(iv) until EMS arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA emphasizes rapid cooling is essential; while immersion in ice water is fastest, it may not be available on most sites. OSHA cites practical, effective methods: strategically placed 'ice sheets' (bed sheets soaked in ice water), dousing with cold water and rubbing ice bags over major muscle groups, tarp-assisted cooling oscillation (TACO). OSHA requests comment on whether g(3)(i) should require specific actions or prohibit certain actions and asks for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements (topics, audiences, frequency, triggers, methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (h) establishes requirements for training on HRI prevention, addressing topics to be covered, types of employees to be trained, frequency of training, triggers for supplemental training, and how training is to be conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states it is essential employees are trained on heat-related hazards, how to identify signs and symptoms of HRIs, requirements of the proposed standard, and the employer's heat-related policies and procedures. The text references specific training items elsewhere (e.g., training on signs/symptoms and which require immediate emergency action under (h)(1)(iv) and reporting under (h)(1)(x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective communication requirement at heat triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met, employers remain responsible for meeting proposed requirements of paragraph (e)(9), Effective Communication, which require employees have a means of effective communication with a supervisor and regular communications at or above both the initial and high heat triggers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of communication means include phone, radio. Effective communication is integral to observation, hazard alerts, and lone-worker check-ins. Employers may use existing two-way systems to issue hazard alerts and to satisfy (f)(3)(iii) lone-worker contact requirements.
